You are a research assistant answering questions about a fixed set of papers.
The papers are plain-text files in your working directory. Explore them with the tools:
- bash: read-only shell (ls, grep -n, find, head, tail, wc, nl, cat, sed -n 'A,Bp')
- read(path, offset, limit): read a file with line numbers

Rules:
- Answer ONLY from text you have actually read in this session. Do not answer from memory.
- If the papers do not contain the answer, say so explicitly instead of guessing.
- When you have enough evidence, reply with your final answer and make NO tool call.
- Support every factual claim with a verbatim quote copied exactly from the source, in the form: "exact text" (file). Never paraphrase inside the quotation marks. A statement that the document(s) do not contain the requested information needs no citation.
- State only what the document(s) say. Do not add background knowledge, general advice, or your own
  conclusions. If the user asks for something the text only partly covers, answer the covered part
  and say plainly which part the document does not address.
- Do not expand abbreviations, name entities, or add details that the text itself does not give.
- Do not end with a summary that recombines earlier points ("In short", "Overall"); the points stand on their own.
- When the user describes their own situation, say what the document states that applies to it; do not
  draw a personal conclusion that the document does not state itself.
- After you give an answer, an automatic check verifies your citations. If you then receive a
  <verification> message, you are in revision mode: fix ONLY the flagged problems by calling
  edit_draft(old, new), where `old` is an exact, unique substring of your previous answer.
  Keep everything else unchanged, and reply "Done" when finished.
  Never call edit_draft before you have given an answer.

When can a person give consent to process their data?

In your answer, refer only to the document in the file `doc.txt`. Do not employ any outside knowledge.

Based on `doc.txt`, the document addresses consent to processing in the following terms:

**Consent as a lawful basis**
- Processing is lawful where "the data subject has given consent to the processing of his or her personal data for one or more specific purposes" (doc.txt).

**Conditions for consent (Article 7)**
- "Where processing is based on consent, the controller shall be able to demonstrate that the data subject has consented to processing of his or her personal data" (doc.txt).
- If consent is given in a written declaration that also concerns other matters, "the request for consent shall be presented in a manner which is clearly distinguishable from the other matters, in an intelligible and easily accessible form, using clear and plain language" (doc.txt).
- Consent must be freely given: "When assessing whether consent is freely given, utmost account shall be taken of whether, inter alia, the performance of a contract, including the provision of a service, is conditional on consent to the processing of personal data that is not necessary for the performance of that contract" (doc.txt).
- "The data subject shall have the right to withdraw his or her consent at any time... Prior to giving consent, the data subject shall be informed thereof. It shall be as easy to withdraw as to give consent" (doc.txt).

**Children (Article 8)**
- For information society services offered directly to a child, "the processing of the personal data of a child shall be lawful where the child is at least 16 years old. Where the child is below the age of 16 years, such processing shall be lawful only if and to the extent that consent is given or authorised by the holder of parental responsibility over the child" (doc.txt). Member States may set a lower age, "provided that such lower age is not below 13 years" (doc.txt).

**Special categories of data (Article 9)**
- Processing of special categories of personal data is prohibited unless, among other grounds, "the data subject has given explicit consent to the processing of those personal data for one or more specified purposes, except where Union or Member State law provide that the prohibition referred to in paragraph 1 may not be lifted by the data subject" (doc.txt).
- Conversely, processing to protect vital interests may occur "where the data subject is physically or legally incapable of giving consent" (doc.txt).

The document does not state any further conditions on when a person may give consent beyond these provisions.
